title: Federal Election Commission v. Akins
summary: Voters could challenge the FEC’s refusal to treat AIPAC as a political committee because denial of useful statutory disclosure information was a concrete injury even though widely shared.

sections.Parties: The respondents were voters whose views often opposed those of the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee. They sought review of the Federal Election Commission’s dismissal of their administrative complaint. The FEC defended its interpretation of federal campaign-finance disclosure requirements and challenged the voters’ standing.
sections.Material Facts: The Federal Election Campaign Act imposed registration, recordkeeping, and disclosure obligations on political committees. The voters alleged that AIPAC’s qualifying expenditures exceeded the statutory threshold and required disclosure of donors and election-related spending. The FEC applied a major-purpose limitation and characterized AIPAC as an issue-oriented lobbying group rather than a political committee. The voters asserted that the missing information would help them evaluate candidates and AIPAC’s role in elections.
sections.Procedural History: The FEC dismissed the administrative complaint. The district court entered summary judgment for the agency, and a divided court-of-appeals panel affirmed. The en banc appellate court reversed on the statutory major-purpose issue. The Supreme Court granted the government’s petition. The assigned selection addresses standing and omits the opinion’s complete disposition and further treatment of the statutory merits.
sections.Issue: Whether voters denied allegedly required campaign information were aggrieved parties and suffered a concrete, traceable, redressable injury, despite the availability of that same information to the broader public and the FEC’s enforcement discretion.
sections.Holding: The voters satisfied the statutory and constitutional standing requirements. Their informational injury was concrete and particular enough for Article III even though widely shared. The statutory review provision also displaced the general presumption against review of agency nonenforcement in this setting. That conclusion authorized review; it did not itself conclusively resolve every merits issue.
sections.Reasoning: The majority read Congress’s authorization of review by an aggrieved complainant in light of the statute’s disclosure purposes. The voters sought information useful to their exercise of voting rights, rather than only an abstract declaration that government obey the law. The breadth of the affected population therefore did not defeat injury. The Court distinguished Richardson’s constitutional taxpayer challenge and treated the specific statutory right as significant. Causation and redressability survived the possibility that the FEC could exercise lawful discretion to reach the same ultimate result: a decision resting on an erroneous legal ground can be set aside and reconsidered. Scalia, joined by O’Connor and Thomas, read aggrievement more narrowly and saw the suit as a demand for third-party enforcement masquerading as an informational claim. He also argued that Richardson was materially indistinguishable and that generalized enforcement suits intruded on executive authority. The source preserves that disagreement; the dissent’s executive-power account does not replace the majority’s holding.
